facts.claim: "Alone (Reprise)" is track 4 on Ryan Harris's 7-song, roughly 19-minute Same Sun EP, released March 24, 2023 on Whitegold Records.
Ryan J Harris is credited as songwriter (composition and lyrics) of "Alone (Reprise)", and Tyler Neil Johnson is credited as producer (production and engineering).
Deezer credits Ryan J Harris as writer and composer of "Alone (Reprise)", which runs about 1:52.

Producer Tyler Neil Johnson's site lists Harris as a client, with roles of producer, mixer, engineer, arranger and instrumentalist. It describes Same Sun as his debut EP, released independently in 2023.
"Alone (Reprise)" follows "Alone" on the EP, and both songs appear on Harris's limited-run 12-inch vinyl "My Mind".

Harris says the Same Sun EP is personal to him. He spent his early life seeking external solutions to internal issues, which didn't work, and he came to see that those issues travel with you wherever you go.
Harris makes his music in a bedroom or home studio in Whistler, BC. His bio describes him as a Canadian filmmaker and musician.
Harris grew up in Canada, New Zealand and Australia, and his family settled back in Canada when he was 15. He started writing folk music for his own film projects in 2021.
Harris opened for the folk duo Ocie Elliott in 2023 and later headlined sold-out tours in Europe, South Africa and Canada in 2025–26.
His original music has passed 100 million streams across all platforms, and his songs have been used in adventure and surf films.

research.lineage: Harris's songs sit in the bedroom-produced indie-folk tradition, and his own bio and tour pages compare him to Ben Howard, Jack Johnson, Ocie Elliott and Gregory Alan Isakov.

draft:
A reprise usually comes at the end of a record, a last look back before the lights come up. **Alone (Reprise)** sits at the center of Ryan Harris's seven-song *Same Sun* EP, track four, right after "Alone." That placement matters. It means Harris returns to the same subject almost immediately, with the dust barely settled. It runs under two minutes, which makes it feel less like a second song and more like the thought you keep having after you've said what you meant to say.

Harris has been plain about what drives the EP. He calls it personal, and describes years of looking for outside fixes to inside problems, then realizing those problems come along wherever you go. That idea fits a reprise. You leave the subject, and it's waiting at the next track. The feeling isn't panic or heartbreak. It's quieter: recognizing that the weight you hoped to set down is still in your hands, and deciding to keep walking with it anyway.

The sound carries that steadiness. An acoustic guitar runs a fingerpicked, arpeggiated pattern, rolling and unhurried. A bass holds simple, sustained notes underneath, more anchor than melody. The drums play light, with a slight swing, kick, snare and hi-hat keeping a moderate pulse that never presses. Harris sings in a clear mid-range, smooth and melodic, with no harmonies stacked behind. One voice, alone, which suits the title without overplaying it. The parts hold their ground rather than swelling or pulling back, and that restraint is the point. The song doesn't dramatize being alone. It just stays in the room with it.

That room is open and clean, a little reverb on everything, every instrument set apart from the others. Harris makes his music in a bedroom or home studio in Whistler, BC, and Tyler Neil Johnson is credited with production and engineering. Their polish is the gentle kind. Harris's own pages put him beside Ben Howard, Jack Johnson, Ocie Elliott and Gregory Alan Isakov, and you can hear the bedroom-folk lineage in that easy, swung brushwork and the uncluttered guitar. What he borrows is the calm. What he bends is the subject: that warm, sunlit sound turned toward something harder to face.

Harris started writing folk songs in 2021 for his own films. This one plays like a held shot, the camera staying on someone after everyone else has left the frame.

It sticks because it sounds like making peace with a problem you can't outrun, and the steadiness lets you admit you're carrying one too.
